machine: 1 laptop: Intel i5-10310U 4 cores / 8 threads, 15.7 GB RAM (about 3 GB free), one engine, Vite dev servers
verdictLine: The platform holds 50,000 people, forecasts every group in seconds and, when a group is solved one at a time and whole, produces schedules with zero rule breaks. It is not ready for an organisation this size: the engine crashed 15 times, every group large enough to need splitting failed, all 12 builds failed when started together, and the gateway stopped answering everyone for 40+ minutes while large schedules were prepared. Four employee features silently stop at 2,000 people.

defects.title: Engine crashes on large solves and takes every running build down with it
defects.steps: Schedule groups of 3,000–6,000 people (one week, 90 s limit). Runs: 12 groups together; then one at a time; then one at a time without splitting.
defects.expected: A solve that runs out of time or memory fails alone; the engine keeps serving
defects.actual: 15 engine crashes in the scale run (engine-supervisor.log; 17 counting the 2 earlier in the day). All 12 builds started together failed. One at a time: every group that the gateway splits into parts (S02, S03, S05 and the split runs of S09, S11) crashed the engine; S10 survived one crash. Logs: 'Fatal Python error: Aborted' (14; 2 of them show SCIP 'Insufficient memory for allocation' followed by an OR-Tools 'Check failed' abort), and one 'Windows fatal exception: access violation' in backends.py respond() while building the reply. The parts of one group are solved side by side in one engine process, each CP-SAT model plus the HiGHS/SCIP backups in memory at once.
defects.evidence: scale/engine-run-*.log, engine-supervisor.log; S11 whole: DONE 157 s, no crash; S11 in parts: crash
defects.fix: Solve each part/solve in its own child process with a memory cap so a native abort kills one solve, not the server; skip the MIP backups (HiGHS/SCIP) above a candidate size they cannot handle; run parts one after another when memory is short; supervise the engine and retry the job after a restart.

defects.title: Preparing a large schedule freezes the gateway for every user
defects.steps: Start schedule builds for groups of 5,000–6,000 people; call GET /health and the admin app meanwhile
defects.expected: The API stays responsive while schedules are built in the background
defects.actual: Gateway pinned at 100% of one CPU core (Node main thread, 430→604 MB); /health timed out at 15–30 s continuously for 40+ minutes; DB sessions sat 'idle in transaction' waiting for the gateway; S03 spent 16 minutes preparing. Opening Schedule Quality for a 6,000-person group did the same for 2+ minutes.
defects.evidence: health-samples.jsonl; scheduleRoutes.ts ~598–640: candidates are built on the main thread, rebuilt up to 8 times at coarser settings, yielding only every 25 people
defects.fix: Build candidates in a worker thread or in the engine; compute the candidate count arithmetically and pick the thinning level once instead of rebuilding the list; cap per-request CPU for report screens and cache their results.

defects.title: An over-limit schedule request is not refused — it runs 8½ minutes and then drops
defects.steps: S13: one template with every 15-minute start and every length 4–12 h, 3,000 people, POST /scheduling/versions
defects.expected: Immediate 400: 'too many possible shifts' (the 900,000 limit exists in the code)
defects.actual: 510 s, then the connection failed; /health afterwards showed Redis down; the gateway answered nobody meanwhile
defects.fix: Estimate people × days × starts × lengths before building and refuse at once.

defects.title: Employee list stops at 2,000 people without saying so
defects.steps: GET /workforce/employees (or ?groupId= for a 6,000-person group); open Workforce › Employees
defects.expected: Paging, or a total and a 'showing 2,000 of 50,000' notice
defects.actual: Exactly 2,000 rows, no total, no next page (loadEmployees … LIMIT 2000). The other 48,000 people cannot be found by scrolling.
defects.fix: Server-side paging with a total count; AG Grid server-side row model.

defects.title: Bulk edit silently skips anyone outside the first 2,000
defects.steps: POST /workforce/employees/bulk with one person inside and one outside the first 2,000 (by last name)
defects.evidence: cap-check.mjs; workforceRoutes.ts:178 uses the capped loader
defects.fix: Load the selected ids directly (WHERE id = ANY($1)) instead of the capped list.

defects.title: Re-importing existing employees fails once the organisation has more than 2,000 people
defects.steps: Import a CSV row for an existing employee outside the first 2,000
defects.expected: Dry run says UPDATE; commit updates them
defects.actual: Dry run says NEW; commit fails with 409 'That already exists' and rejects the whole file. A nightly HR sync of 50,000 people cannot run.
defects.fix: Match existing employees by number with a direct query for the numbers in the file.

defects.title: The 'two builds at a time' limit is not enforced
defects.steps: Queue 12 schedule jobs while the gateway is busy
defects.actual: 10 jobs RUNNING at once on one gateway, multiplying the load that caused DEF-29 and DEF-30
defects.evidence: schedule_jobs rows at 14:35; scheduleJobs.ts tick(): the running-count check and the claim are separated by an await, and tick() runs from both a timer and every enqueue
defects.fix: Make tick() single-flight (a flag or mutex) and claim only CONCURRENCY - running.size jobs in one UPDATE.

defects.title: Jobs fail at once while the engine restarts, and timeouts are reported as 'engine not reachable'
defects.steps: Queue jobs during the ~60 s an engine takes to start; or solve a group whose call exceeds the gateway's gRPC deadline
defects.expected: Wait/retry with back-off; a timeout says it timed out
defects.actual: 8 jobs failed within 5 s each; S09 (no crash) failed after 172 s with 'The forecasting engine is not reachable'
defects.fix: Retry engine-unavailable failures with back-off for a few minutes; distinguish DEADLINE_EXCEEDED from UNAVAILABLE in the message.

defects.title: At 3,000+ people the optimiser adds nothing: schedules are the greedy starting roster
defects.steps: Schedule any group with ≥ 210,000 candidate shifts (S01, S06, S08, S11, S12, S13) with a 90 s limit
defects.expected: CP-SAT improves on the starting roster; or the screen says the result is unoptimised
defects.actual: Every one: 'cpsat: feasible (starting roster only), highs: unknown, scip: unknown, greedy: feasible', gap 1 (100%). Valid schedules, often 95–98% covered, but contract hours, preferences and fairness are not optimised. Only S04/S07 (≤ 75,000 candidates) were optimised.
defects.fix: Split earlier (smaller parts, solved safely — see DEF-29), give large groups a longer default limit, and show 'starting roster only' prominently on the schedule.

defects.title: Email (24 h turnaround) demand is spread across the night
defects.steps: S04: email queue, weekday office-hours history (no night volume), Mon–Fri 08:00–18:30 templates
defects.expected: Back-office work can wait within its 24 h turnaround, so it is staffed in office hours
defects.actual: Requirement of about 140 people 00:00–08:00 every day; coverage 43.5% while 388,976 surplus quarter-hours sit in the day; shortage report: 'no shift template covers this time'
defects.fix: For deferrable channels, place the requirement within the queue's opening hours (backlog model) instead of flat over 24 h.

defects.title: Full-timers scheduled well below contract hours with no warning
defects.steps: Validate hours per person in S11 (overstaffed) and S01
defects.expected: Contract hours met, or the shortfall listed as a warning for payroll
defects.actual: Full-time 40 h people averaged 21.7 h (S11) and 32.4 h (S01); schedule statistics show warnings: 0
defects.fix: Report contract-hour shortfall per person; offer VTO instead of silently cutting hours where the policy pays contract hours.

defects.title: Screens and reads for a 6,000-person group are slow and heavy
defects.steps: Open screens with the 6,000-person group selected; call the shift and plan APIs
defects.actual: Schedule Timeline 44 s, 236 MB browser heap; Live Coverage and Adherence 30 s; Schedule Quality > 120 s; plan view API 18 s; shifts API returns everything at once (15 MB for one week; 79 MB for 2,000 people × 13 weeks — about 1 GB for 6,000 × 52 weeks)
defects.fix: Page and window the shift APIs (by day/team), virtualise the timeline, precompute report screens.

defects.title: Model choice is not explained: unsuitable models run, unavailable ones fall back quietly
defects.steps: Request ARIMA for S09, Croston for S04, GBM for S06
defects.expected: The screen says what each model needs and warns when the chosen one is worse than a naive forecast
defects.actual: ARIMA used though worse than seasonal naive (MASE 2.6, WAPE 7.7% vs ~0.1–0.2% elsewhere, stability VARIABLE). GBM needs 120 days of history and Croston a sparse daily series; both fell back with a note only in the summary.
defects.fix: Show eligibility next to each model and warn when the selected model loses to the baseline.

defects.title: Publishing a schedule does not notify the people on it
defects.steps: Publish S01 (6,000 people) → sign in as S01-00001
defects.fix: Confirm intended behaviour; if not, notify on publish (batched).

strengths: 50,000 employees loaded through the real API: 6,000-row CSV imports in about 3.5 s, 12 weeks of 15-minute history per queue in about 2 s, 400 leave requests and 400 availability rules without an error.

Every forecast model the engine offers was exercised across 13 groups; each forecast was created in 3–6 s, published through submit/approve/publish, plus a 365-day long-term forecast and a +20% adjustment. Missing days were tolerated and outlier days detected and replaced.

Independent re-check of every shift in 9 built schedules (250,495 shifts, incl. a 13-week plan): 0 double-bookings, 0 rest or weekly-hour breaks, 0 shifts on approved leave, 0 in unavailable hours, 0 weekend shifts for the 1,200 people who may not work weekends, and everyone got shifts.
Solved whole and one at a time, groups of 3,000–6,000 people built in about 3 minutes each (S01: 6,000 people, 98.4% covered).
Rotation 4-on-4-off: 2,000 members assigned in 4 s and 28,000 shifts materialised in 12 s.
Live agent states for 6,000 people accepted in 3 batches of 2,000 (about 330 ms each); the 2,000-per-call limit is enforced with a clear message.
Publishing a 6,000-person schedule (24,288 shifts) took 9.5 s; the employee then saw their week in the portal in under 100 ms.
The shortage report explains gaps in plain words with causes and suggested actions (overtime, a missing template, temporary staff).

parallelRun.note: All 12 jobs queued together (S13 not queued: the orchestrator lost its connection to the frozen gateway). Up to 10 ran at once although the limit is 2.
